summary: In Capernaum, collectors ask whether Jesus pays the temple tax; He teaches Peter that the King’s Son is free, then pays it with a coin from a fish.
key_insight: Jesus claims to be exempt, the Son of the King whose house the temple is, and then pays anyway, “lest we offend them.” He pays with one coin “for Me and you,” putting Peter beside Himself.
story: When Jesus and His disciples came back to Capernaum, the men who collected the temple tax came to Peter and asked, “Does your Teacher not pay the temple tax?” “Yes,” Peter said.
When Peter came into the house, Jesus spoke to him first: “What do you think, Simon? From whom do the kings of the earth take customs or taxes, from their sons or from strangers?”

“From strangers,” Peter answered. Jesus said to him, “Then the sons are free. Nevertheless, lest we offend them, go to the sea, cast in a hook, and take the fish that comes up first. And when you have opened its mouth, you will find a piece of money; take that and give it to them for Me and you.”

scene.label: The temple tax
scene.text: Every Jewish man twenty years and older paid half a shekel a year toward the temple and its sacrifices, a practice based on Exodus 30:13–16. In Jesus’ day it was reckoned as two drachmas, and Matthew’s Greek calls the tax simply the didrachma, the two-drachma.

scene.label: Two days’ pay
scene.text: A drachma was worth about the same as a Roman denarius, a laborer’s daily wage. The tax cost each man about two days’ work.

scene.label: One coin for two
scene.text: The coin in the fish’s mouth was a stater (the NKJV says “a piece of money”), a silver coin worth four drachmas. That was exactly the tax for two men, Jesus and Peter.

scene.label: God’s tax, not Caesar’s
scene.text: This was not a Roman tax but a gift for God’s house, collected in the towns and carried to Jerusalem. Jesus answers a different question, about taxes to Caesar, in the temple during His last week (Matthew 22:15–22).

witnesses.matthew: Matthew, the former tax collector (9:9), alone tells this story. It shows Jesus as the Son of the King, free from the tax, who still chooses not to give needless offense. Matthew ends with Jesus’ instruction and does not describe the catch; Jesus’ word is the point.

seeing.reveals: Jesus speaks as the Son of the King: the temple is His Father’s house, and He owes it nothing. Yet He lays aside His right, and the Lord of the sea supplies the coin.
seeing.living: Jesus was free, and still He chose not to cause needless offense. Christian freedom is real, but love is willing to lay it down for the sake of others (1 Corinthians 9:19). Before insisting on a right, ask whether it will open a door for the gospel or close one.
seeing.ponder: What right or freedom might Jesus be asking you to lay down so that others do not stumble?

preaching.big_idea: The free Son pays what He does not owe, so that others will not stumble.
preaching.watch_for: The argument turns on sons and strangers. It assumes the temple is His Father’s house, the claim Jesus made when He first cleared it (John 2:16). The Greek word behind “offend” returns in the next chapter, where Jesus warns against causing little ones to stumble (Matthew 18:6).
